herdr-pomodoro: a focus timer that knows what I am working on

The problem it solves

Agents made editing so fast that it is tempting to vibe on several projects at the same time: a prompt here, a review there, three agents running in three repositories. Every moment feels productive, but the project that matters gets scraps of attention and every switch costs me the thread. Willpower is a weak tool against a sidebar full of blinking agents. An ordinary pomodoro timer does not help either: it counts minutes, not work, and has no idea what is happening on my screen.

The general idea

I built herdr-pomodoro, a plugin for herdr written in Rust, to enforce the focus instead of hoping for it. A focus session runs for 25 minutes on one workspace. During it the agent list shows only that workspace and the sidebar toggle is locked, so the other projects cannot pull me away. A five-minute break follows and everything is visible again. If I really need to look elsewhere, a three-minute grace period keeps the session alive, and returning in time resumes the original deadline.

Examples

A popup on prefix+ctrl+p adapts to the current phase: start focus, end the session, leave the terminal, use another workspace, return to focus, end the break or open the activity dashboard. From the command line:

herdr-pomodoro status              # does this setup support activity capture?
herdr-pomodoro watch --duration 10 # ten seconds of content-free observations

The plugin is open source: github.com/MarcellGranat/herdr-pomodoro. It needs herdr 0.9.5 or newer and a stable Rust toolchain. To install it:

git clone https://github.com/MarcellGranat/herdr-pomodoro
cd herdr-pomodoro
cargo build --release --locked
herdr plugin link "$PWD" --enabled

On macOS, run ./target/release/herdr-pomodoro reconcile once after linking if you do not restart the herdr server right away. It installs a small per-user LaunchAgent that keeps the watcher running when no plugin pane is open.

Tips from my setup

  • It only counts real human input. The plugin compares access-time changes on the terminal device of the herdr client and of a workspace pane. Input that reaches both is human, input that reaches only the pane comes from an agent. It never reads the content of a terminal, never records keystrokes and stores only timestamps.
  • It works over SSH and mosh, because the input still passes through both devices on the machine that runs herdr. That includes sessions from the phone. Remote workspaces are sampled over SSH without installing anything on the other machine.
  • The timer is always visible. A sidebar token shows the phase and the tab bar shows the countdown, refreshed every second.
  • The sidebar is locked during focus. It starts hidden, and a guard binding blocks the toggle until the session ends, which removes the temptation.
  • Restarts are safe. Deadlines are stored, not recomputed, so the timer survives a restart of the plugin or of herdr.
  • Built with OpenSpec, one small change at a time. See the post about OpenSpec.
